method_card.title: Bar Charts & Line Graphs
steps: Read the axis titles and units first
Find your category or year on the bottom axis
Read across to the side axis, checking the gridline step
Then compare, total or subtract as the question asks
method_card.content:
Bar charts compare separate categories: the taller the bar, the bigger the value. Line graphs show change over time, so they reveal trends, peaks and troughs.

Always check the gridline step before you read a value. A step might be worth 1, 5, 10 or 5,000. Bar tops and plotted points often sit between gridlines, so judge the fraction of the gap.

Stacked bars sit sections on top of each other, so a section's size is the level at its top minus the level below it. Dual charts show two sets of data together, so use the legend to pick the right one before reading.
method_card.example:
Question: A bar chart shows summer rainfall: June 70 mm, July 65 mm, August 75 mm. Find the total.

Step 1: Read each bar top across to the side axis.

Step 2: Add them: 70 + 65 + 75.

Answer: 210 mm

gold.display: The bar chart shows average monthly rainfall for a town. Which statement best describes its rainfall pattern?

Dry summers and wet winters, a Mediterranean pattern
Rain spread evenly through the year
Almost no rain in any month

misconceptions.message: The wettest bars sit at the two ends of the year, not in the middle. Compare the midsummer bars with the midwinter ones.
The bars are far from even: check the shortest bar against the tallest before you decide.

gold.hint: Compare the midsummer bars with the midwinter ones before you choose.

guided_steps.pre: Twelve bars, January to December. Counting from the left, July is bar number
guided_steps.hint: January is bar 1, so count on from there.
guided_steps.say: A pattern question still starts with readings. Take one from midsummer and one from midwinter.

guided_steps.hint: Divide the taller reading by the shorter one.

guided_steps.say: Dry summers, wet winters: that is the Mediterranean pattern. Choose that option.

misconceptions.message: In 1960 both rates are still high and the birth rate has barely moved. Look for where the birth rate begins its steep fall.
By 2000 the birth rate has already been falling for years. Stage 3 starts when that fall begins, not part way through it.

gold.hint: Stage 3 begins where the birth rate line starts falling steeply, after the death rate has already dropped.

problem_bank.bronze_description: Take a single value off a bar top or a plotted point, or pick out the highest or lowest.
problem_bank.silver_description: Take two or more readings, then find a difference, a total, a range or a percentage change.
problem_bank.gold_description: Work with stacked bars and paired data sets, then explain what the pattern shows.

worked_examples.question: A bar chart shows the population of five UK cities. London = 9 million, Birmingham = 1.1 million, Leeds = 0.8 million, Glasgow = 0.6 million, Bristol = 0.5 million. What is the difference between the largest and smallest city?

steps.label: Use geographical language
steps.content: Temperature increases steadily from winter (14°C) to summer (28°C), reaching a peak in July, before declining through autumn and winter.

steps.label: Calculate the range
steps.content: Range = 28 − 14 = 14°C. This shows a large annual temperature range, typical of a hot desert climate.

worked_examples.question: A line graph shows average temperature in Cairo rising from 14°C in January to 28°C in July, then falling to 16°C in December. Describe the trend.

bronze.title: Bronze: one reading, straight off the chart
steps: Start with the axis titles. They tell you what is being measured and in what units.
Find your category or year along the bottom axis, then move up to the bar top or the plotted point.
Slide across to the side axis and read the value. Check the gridline step first, because bar tops often land between labels.

example.question: A bar chart of monthly rainfall. Read the value for March.

silver.title: Silver: two readings, then a calculation
steps: Silver questions need two or more readings, so take each one carefully before you calculate anything.
Use the legend to tell paired bars or lines apart, and read both at the same place on the bottom axis.
Then do the move the question asks for: a difference, a total, a range or a percentage change. Subtract the smaller or earlier value from the larger or later one.

example.question: A dual bar chart of rainfall in two towns. Find the difference in their annual totals.

steps.label: Total the first town
steps.content: Add all twelve of Town A's bars: 620 mm.

steps.label: Total the second
steps.content: Add all twelve of Town B's bars: 480 mm.

gold.title: Gold: stacked bars, two data sets, and what the pattern shows
steps: In a stacked bar each section begins where the last one ended, so a section's size is the level at its top minus the level below.
When two data sets share a chart, check which line or colour belongs to which before you read anything.
Finish by saying what the pattern means: a trend, a lag, a stage, a climate type. Back it up with a number you have read.
